Hook: In 1971 the Dutch economist Jan Pen asked his readers to watch a parade. Everyone in the country marches past in exactly one hour, and each person is as tall as their income: someone with the average income is of average height. Here are American families raising children around the year 2000, one marcher for each percentile, from the tax records. For the first minutes the marchers barely reach your ankles: at minute six they are 29 centimetres tall. At half past, the median family goes by, at 1.17 metres, well below average height. You wait until minute 42 before anyone of average height appears. Then the giants: 2.8 metres at minute fifty-four, 8 metres in the last minute, and in the final seconds the top percentile, 27 metres tall on average.

And Pen's parade does not end there, because the top percentile is itself unequal. Take the tax records for 2022 and put everyone on one scale. The median family is a little over a metre tall, and average height is one metre seventy. The richest one percent of tax units average about 33 metres; the richest one in a thousand, about 147 metres. And the richest one in ten thousand, with 370 times the average income, about 28 million dollars a year, are over 600 metres tall, taller than any building in America. Their heads are in the clouds.

This part asks how unequal incomes and wealth are, why, and whether children escape where they started. How should inequality be measured, and what does each measure hide? Why do incomes and wealth have such long tails, and why did the tails grow? Do children escape their parents' place in the parade, and in which parts of America do they? And what has happened to the distribution of the whole world, and does any of it matter?
Economics, Built. Part forty: inequality and mobility.

Here is the plan. A game, then the measures and the ethics inside them, and a century of top incomes. Where Pareto's long tails come from, and why they moved so fast. Wealth, and Piketty's r against g; Kuznets's curve. Then mobility: the elasticity between generations, forty million tax records, and the places where children rise. Finally the world, whether inequality matters, two dials, the distributional tables that analysts build, and the frontier.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: four numbers.

Your turn. Four numbers about America, and a guess for each before the answers. First: of all the income Americans received in 2022, what share went to the richest one percent? Second: of all household wealth, what share do the richest one percent of households hold? Third: a child whose parents are in the bottom fifth of the income distribution. What is the chance that, as an adult, the child reaches the top fifth? And fourth: of Americans born in 1984, what share earn more at thirty than their parents did at the same age, after inflation? Pause, and write down your four guesses.

Here are the answers. The richest one percent received 19.6 percent of all pre-tax income in 2022, about one dollar in five; counting capital gains, 23.6 percent. They hold 32.5 percent of all household wealth, about a third. A child from the bottom fifth has a 7.5 percent chance of reaching the top fifth; if parents did not matter at all, it would be twenty. And of children born in 1984, only 50 percent out-earn their parents, against 92 percent of those born in 1940. Keep your guesses: each of these numbers has a chapter.
Measures: Part three drew the Lorenz curve; here it is again, for two thousand of the Island's incomes. Line everyone up from poorest to richest and plot the share of income held by each poorest fraction. With perfect equality the curve is the diagonal. The Gini index is twice the area between them: here 0.41. Every measure is an estimate from a sample, so each deserves a standard error. Resampling the two thousand incomes gives about 0.012 for the Gini, and for the top one percent's share, 9.4 percent, about 1 point: the very top is always measured least precisely, because so few people are in it.

For American households, the Census Bureau has computed the Gini every year since 1967, from its survey. It was 0.40 in 1967, and 0.49 in 2025: a large rise, most of it in the 1980s and 1990s. Surveys have limits: few very rich households answer them, and the income counted is before taxes and most transfers. Chapter three turns to the tax records instead.

In 1970 Anthony Atkinson pointed out that every index of inequality hides a judgement about how much inequality matters. He made the judgement explicit. Value each income by a concave function, with a parameter epsilon for aversion to inequality, and ask: what income, given equally to everyone, would be as good as the actual distribution? With epsilon zero, only the total counts: the answer is the mean, 60,000 dollars. With epsilon one half, 51,313 dollars: society would give up 14 percent of income for equality. With epsilon one, 44,706 dollars; with two, 32,994 dollars; with four, a society that cares almost only about its poorest, 12,212 dollars. Atkinson's index is the share given up. The data cannot choose epsilon; that is ethics.

Measures can disagree, and the reason is that Lorenz curves can cross. Two societies of ten. In A, four people are poor and the other six have the same income. In B, one person is rich and the other nine are alike. The curves cross. Their Gini indices are identical. The top ten percent's share calls B far more unequal: its rich person takes more than a third. Atkinson's index with a mild aversion to inequality agrees, just. With a strong aversion, it calls A far more unequal, because it weighs the poorest most. When curves cross, there is no ranking without a value judgement: one more reason to report several measures, and to say which part of the distribution each one watches.
Top: Chapter three. A century of top incomes.

Surveys miss the top; tax records do not, at least for the income that is taxed. In 2003 Thomas Piketty and Emmanuel Saez used American income tax returns, which exist from 1913, to measure the shares of the top for ninety years, and Saez has kept the series going. The top ten percent's share was 46 percent on the eve of the 1929 crash. It collapsed during the Second World War, and stayed near a third for four decades. The top one percent's share fell from 20 percent to about 8. Then, from about 1980, both rose again: by 2022 the top ten percent took 50 percent, and the top one percent 20, back where they were in the 1920s. A U-shape over the century: the compression came fast, in war and depression, and the widening came within a generation.

The same method has now been applied in dozens of countries, gathered in the World Inequality Database. Its series measure all of national income, so their levels differ a little from the tax series. In America and Britain, the top one percent's share traces a U. In France, Sweden and Germany it fell just as far in the first half of the century, but rose much less afterwards: more an L than a U. The same technology reached all of them, so technology alone cannot explain the difference; Piketty and Saez point to taxes on top incomes and to how pay is set at the top. In China after 1978, India after 1991 and Russia after 1991, the share rose steeply as markets opened: in Russia it went from under six percent in 1989 to over twenty by 2000; in India it more than doubled after 1991.

How much did the top really pull away? The measurement is disputed. On the income reported on tax returns, the top one percent's share rose from 9 to 19 percent between 1962 and 2019. But a third of that came around the tax reform of 1986, when many business owners moved profits from corporate to personal returns; on one reading, much of that income moved rather than grew. Piketty, Saez and Zucman allocate all of national income, and find the top share of income after taxes and transfers rising from 9 to 15 percent. Gerald Auten and David Splinter, two government tax economists, make different assumptions about whose untaxed income it is, and find a rise of only 2.6 points before tax since the early 1960s, and 1.4 points after taxes and transfers since 1979. Both sides use the same tax returns. They differ over income that no return records, such as retained profits and underreported business income, and over how to count transfers. Whoever is right, the lesson is that a top share is a construction, and the assumptions belong on the label.
Pareto: Chapter four. Pareto tails and random growth.

In 1896 Vilfredo Pareto, working through tax records from several countries, noticed that the number of people with incomes above x fell like x to a fixed power, minus alpha. If that holds, the share of income held by the richest fraction p is proportional to p to the power one minus one over alpha: on logarithmic scales, a straight line. Here are America's top shares in 1970, from the top ten percent to the top one in ten thousand. A straight line, with slope 0.59: alpha about 2.4. In 2022, another straight line, flatter, with alpha about 1.6. The smaller alpha, the fatter the tail: within the top one percent, the top tenth then holds a larger share, and the same again within that tenth. The tail looks the same at every scale.

From the ratio of two top shares, each year's alpha follows. In 1928 it was 1.61, a fat tail. The tail thinned through the war and after, to 2.63 in 1962. Since then it has fattened again, to 1.56 in 2022. Pareto's law has held for a century; what moves is its exponent. Why should incomes have such a tail at all?

The answer most economists now give goes back to David Champernowne in 1953: random growth. On the Island, each year every income changes by a random percentage, a promotion, a bad year, a lucky client, with a spread of 14 percent, and no one falls below a floor of a third of the starting income. Here are five careers that start at the same income. Percentage changes compound: after forty years, 2 of the five earn less than when they started, and one earns 5 times as much. Careers end, on average after forty years, and newcomers start again at the bottom. Without that, incomes would spread out for ever; with it, the distribution settles down.

Simulate 50,000 careers for three centuries, until the distribution stops changing. On logarithmic scales, the share of people above each income falls on a straight line: a Pareto tail, from nothing but compounding luck and turnover. Why a straight line? Write y for log income and f for its density. f changes because incomes drift, because they spread, because careers end, and because newcomers enter: the Kolmogorov forward equation. In the stationary state, above the entry point, the solution is an exponential in y, which is a power law in income. Substituting gives a quadratic for the exponent zeta. With the Island's numbers, zeta is 1.55; the simulation agrees, and the top one percent take about 20 percent of income. The formula says what fattens the tail: more volatile incomes, faster average growth at the top, or longer careers.

That makes Pareto tails one of the series' facts. In the data, top incomes follow Pareto's law, with an exponent that moves. The theory: proportional random growth with turnover. And Agora's Kolmogorov equation gives the tail its simulated careers produce.
Speed: Chapter five. Why the tail moved so fast.

Random growth explains the shape of the tail. Can it explain how fast the tail changed? In America, the top one percent's share more than doubled between the late 1970s and the mid 2000s. On the Island, raise the volatility of incomes enough to move the top share from about seven percent to twenty, and watch the Kolmogorov equation carry the distribution to its new state. It crawls: half of the change in the log of the top share takes 57 years, because the tail fills only as careers that began long ago drift upward. In 2016 Xavier Gabaix, Jean-Michel Lasry, Pierre-Louis Lions and Benjamin Moll showed that the standard model is far too slow. Their repair: let a few people be high-growth types, a founder, a star, whose income grows fast for a while before they become ordinary. Make those types grow faster, and the top share moves in time with the data: half of the change in 18 years.

Gabaix and his coauthors found two ways to speed the model up. Scale dependence: growth rates that rise with income itself, as when the best performers reach ever larger markets, the superstars of Part thirty-nine. Type dependence: a group whose incomes grow fast for a time, as in theories of superstar entrepreneurs and managers. On the Island, speeding up the high-growth types moves their own tail exponent from 2.3 to 1.3. The two differ in what they predict for the growth of top incomes, year by year, which is why the question moved to panel data that follow the same top earners over time.
Wealth: Chapter six. Wealth, and r against g.

Wealth is far more concentrated than income. The Federal Reserve now splits all American household wealth, every quarter since 1989. The richest one percent held 22.8 percent in 1989, and 32.5 percent in 2026. The next nine percent held between 34 and 40 percent throughout. The middle forty percent, the homeowners, fell from 36 to 29 percent. And the bottom half of American households together own 2.3 percent of the wealth: less than a tenth of what the top one percent own.

Wealth has a Pareto tail too. From the shares of the top one and top ten percent, the exponent follows. It was 1.74 in 1989, and 1.48 in 2026: fatter, and fatter than the tail of incomes. Physicists who fitted the Forbes 400 lists of the richest Americans from 1988 to 2003 found 1.49, close to what the top shares imply now. Why is wealth's tail so fat?

In 2014 Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century put one inequality at the centre: r greater than g. When the return on wealth exceeds the growth rate of the economy, inherited wealth grows faster than incomes, unless it is consumed or taxed. Random growth makes the argument precise. A dynasty's wealth, relative to the economy, grows at r minus g minus what it consumes, with luck in its returns, and dynasties end or split. The tail exponent of wealth then depends on r minus g. With r equal to g, zeta is 3.2 on the Island. At two points, 1.8; at three, 1.3. A point or two of r minus g turns a thin tail into a very fat one; past a threshold, wealth has no stable distribution at all.

The book drew sharp replies. Matthew Rognlie found that most of the rise in the net share of income going to capital is housing, not factories or shares. Per Krusell and Anthony Smith showed that, once capital wears out, the ratio of wealth to income does not explode as growth slows. And a rising capital share as capital piles up requires capital and labour to be easy substitutes, with an elasticity above one, while most estimates are below it. What survives is the mechanism: what matters for the tail is the return earned by the very top, and how it compares with the growth of everyone else's income.
Kuznets: In December 1954 Simon Kuznets gave his presidential address to the American Economic Association. His argument was arithmetic. Picture a country where most people farm, with low and fairly equal incomes, and a modern sector in the cities, with higher and more unequal ones. When everyone farms, inequality is modest: on the Island, a Gini of 0.22. As people move to the cities, the gap between the sectors adds inequality, most of all when the population is split in half: the Gini peaks at 0.44. When nearly everyone has moved, the gap stops mattering, and the Gini falls back to 0.38. The variance of log income makes the reason plain: the term for the gap between sectors is largest when the shares are equal. Growth first widens inequality, then narrows it: an inverted U.

Kuznets was candid about his evidence: a few series for America, Britain and Germany. He called the paper perhaps five percent empirical information and ninety-five percent speculation. What he could see was the downslope: the American top ten percent's share had fallen from 46 percent in 1928. The tax records since show what came next: the share stayed low until the 1970s, then climbed back to 50 percent, long after America had finished industrializing. And the fall he saw was concentrated in depression and war, when capital incomes collapsed and taxes rose, not spread over decades of migration.

Called it? In 1954 Kuznets predicted that inequality widens in the early phases of growth, as people leave the land, and narrows later. In rich countries inequality did narrow until the 1970s, but mostly through depression, war and policy, not migration; and from about 1980 it widened again in America and Britain, long after industrialization. Within countries that are still urbanizing, his arithmetic still bites. The verdict: partly right. The mechanism is real; the law is not.
IGE: Chapter eight. Like parent, like child? The elasticity and the Gatsby curve.

Now the second half of the question: do children escape where they started? The classic measure is the intergenerational elasticity, beta: regress children's log income on their parents'. A beta of zero-point-four means a parent earning twice as much as another has children earning about a third more. Here are six hundred of the Island's families, where the truth is planted: beta is 0.45. But estimate it with one year of the parents' income, as early studies did, and you get 0.24: families look more mobile than they are. One year of income is permanent income plus a good or bad year, and the noise flattens the slope.

The fix is to average. With T years of parents' income, the transitory part shrinks by T, and the estimate climbs towards the truth by exactly the factor in this formula. On the Island: 0.24 with one year, 0.38 with five, 0.42 with fifteen. This is the history of the American estimates. Early studies with a single year found about 0.2, and concluded that America was very mobile. In 1992 Gary Solon averaged several years and found 0.4 or higher. In 2005 Bhashkar Mazumder used long spells of fathers' Social Security earnings, and found about 0.6. Measurement error had made America look more mobile than it was.

Across countries, the elasticity runs from below 0.2 in Denmark, Norway and Finland to almost 0.7 in Peru, and Miles Corak showed in 2013 that it is higher where inequality is higher. Alan Krueger named the pattern the Great Gatsby curve. Why might they go together? On the Island, build economies that differ in one thing only: how much the labour market pays for skill. Skill is partly inherited, and luck is not. Where skill pays more, incomes spread out, and because skill runs in families, parents' incomes predict their children's more closely: the economies line up on a Gatsby curve. The curve need not mean that inequality causes immobility; one cause can produce both.

The curve appears within America too. Here are the country's commuting zones, local labour markets, sized by population. Across, the inequality of incomes among the bottom ninety-nine percent; up, how high a child from a family at the twenty-fifth percentile is expected to rise. The correlation is minus 0.42: in more unequal places, children from poorer families rise less. Where those numbers come from is the subject of the next two chapters.

The Gatsby curve is one of the series' facts. In the data, more unequal countries, and more unequal American places, have less mobility. One theory: a high return to skills that families pass on. And in Agora, raising only that return moves an economy up the curve, from a Gini of 0.30 and an elasticity of 0.08 to 0.61 and 0.42.
Chetty: Chapter nine. Forty million tax records.

In 2014 Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Patrick Kline and Emmanuel Saez linked the tax records of more than forty million American children to their parents'. Instead of logs, they used ranks: each child's place in the income distribution of their own generation, against the parents' place in theirs. Here are children born from 1980 to 1982, grouped by their parents' percentile. The relation is a straight line, with a slope of 0.341: ten percentiles richer parents, three and a half percentiles higher children. If parents did not matter, the line would be flat at fifty. Ranks do not suffer from zero incomes, or from the very top, the way logs do, which is why the rank slope is now the standard measure.

Summing their transition matrix by fifths gives the chances behind the line. Each row is a group of parents; each cell, the percent of their children who end up in each fifth. A child born to the bottom fifth reaches the top fifth with probability 7.5 percent: the third answer of the game. A third of those children stay in the bottom fifth. And 37 percent of the children of the top fifth stay there. If parents' incomes did not matter, every cell would read twenty.

Relative mobility asks who climbs past whom. Absolute mobility asks something plainer: do children earn more than their parents did at the same age, after inflation? In 2017 Chetty and five coauthors traced it by birth year. For children born in 1940, 92 percent out-earned their parents. For those born in 1984, 50 percent: a coin toss. By parents' percentile: over ninety percent of the 1940 cohort out-earned their parents at almost every level, and 88 percent even at the ninetieth percentile. For the 1984 cohort the line has fallen everywhere, and further the richer the parents.

Why the fall? Two things changed: the economy grew more slowly, and its growth went increasingly to the top. The authors separate them. For children born in 1980, absolute mobility was 50 percent. Restore the faster growth of the 1940s and 1950s, but share it as it is shared now, and it rises only to 62 percent. Keep today's slower growth, but share it as it was shared for the 1940 cohort, and it rises to 80 percent. Most of the fading American dream is the distribution of growth, not its rate.
Places: The tax records also say where each child grew up. For every commuting zone, the authors computed upward mobility: the expected rank, as an adult, of a child whose parents were at the twenty-fifth percentile. It varies enormously across America. In the places at the tenth percentile, such a child is expected to reach rank 37; at the ninetieth, rank 52. That gap is as large as the gap, nationally, between children whose parents are about 43 percentiles apart.

Among the fifty largest places, the extremes are striking. In Charlotte, a child from the bottom fifth has a 4.4 percent chance of reaching the top fifth; in Atlanta, Raleigh and Indianapolis, about five. In Boston, Pittsburgh and Salt Lake City, about ten; in San Jose, 12.9: three times Charlotte's chance.

What do the high-mobility places have in common? Here are the correlations of upward mobility with characteristics of each place. The strongest negative ones: the share of children raised by single mothers, the share of Black residents, inequality, and segregation, by race and by income. The positive ones: a large middle class, short commutes, social capital, religious participation, better schools. The authors summarized five factors: segregation, inequality, schools, social capital and family structure. These are correlations across places. Is it the places themselves, or the families who live there?

Two designs answer that. Chetty and Hendren followed millions of families who moved, and compared siblings and children who moved at different ages. Children's outcomes converge to those of the place they move to at about 4 percent a year of childhood spent there: what matters is how long, not just where. And in the Moving to Opportunity experiment of the 1990s, families in public housing in five cities won, by lottery, vouchers to move to lower-poverty neighbourhoods. Children who moved before thirteen earned 3,477 dollars a year more in their mid-twenties, 31 percent more than the control group. Those who moved as teenagers did not gain. Places matter, and they matter most early.
World: Step back to the whole world. The largest part of global inequality is between countries: where you are born. Treat everyone as earning their country's average, and compute a Gini across the world's people. It was 0.64 in 1980, and 0.47 in 2023: a large fall. Take China out, and most of the fall disappears. Take out India as well, and inequality between the remaining countries did not fall at all. Since 1980 China's output per person has grown about 22-fold, India's 6-fold. Two countries with a third of humanity moved from the bottom of the world's distribution towards its middle.

Inside the world distribution, Christoph Lakner and Branko Milanovic ranked everyone on one scale and asked how much real income grew at each percentile between 1988 and 2008. Plotted, the curve looks like an elephant raising its trunk. The largest gains were around the global median, mostly the new middle classes of China and the rest of Asia. Around the 80th to 85th percentiles, largely the lower middle classes of rich countries, there was essentially no gain. And the global top one percent gained a great deal. The curve compares positions, not people: the person at a percentile in 2008 is not the one who was there in 1988. Still, it tells the political story of the period, and Part thirty-six's China shock is one of its chapters.

The World Inequality Database estimates the share of the world's top one percent, from scattered points in the nineteenth century to yearly figures since 1980. About 26 percent in 1910; 15 percent in 1970; 21 percent in 2024. Two forces pull in opposite directions: poorer countries catching up shrinks the gaps between nations, while rising inequality inside many of them pulls the top away.
Matters: Does any of this matter, beyond the numbers? Start with the starkest. Linking tax records to death records, Chetty and coauthors measured life expectancy by income. At forty, the richest one percent of American men can expect to live 14.6 years longer than the poorest one percent; for women, 10.1 years. Between 2001 and 2014 the gap widened. But a gradient is not an effect of inequality. Income buys health, and health earns income: illness lowers earnings as surely as poverty raises illness. Whether a more unequal society is less healthy, holding each person's own income fixed, is a different and much harder question.

The same difficulty runs through every claim about inequality's consequences. For growth: regressions of growth on inequality across countries have found positive, negative and no effects, depending on the period, the sample and the method; countries differ in too many other ways. For health: a person's own income clearly matters; the effect of other people's incomes is very hard to separate from everything else that differs between places. For politics: the rich vote, give and lobby more, and whether policy follows their preferences more closely is a live debate. What has worked is the toolkit of Part four: lotteries, reforms, local shocks and moves, like the movers of chapter ten. Inequality matters most clearly where it shapes opportunity.
Tools: What can a society do? The textbook distinction is between redistribution and pre-distribution. Redistribution changes incomes after the market has set them. Start with market income: wages, profits, interest and rents. Subtract taxes, the subject of Part forty-one. Add cash transfers, the subject of Part forty-two. Add services in kind, such as health care and schools. Even the simplest scheme is powerful: on the Island, a flat tax of 20 percent paid back equally to everyone lowers the Gini from 0.41 to 0.32. What it costs in work and saving is Part forty-one's question.

Pre-distribution changes what the market pays in the first place. Skills, through schools and early childhood, the race of Part thirty-nine. How wages are set: minimum wages and unions. Competition, against the market power of Parts ten and thirty-eight. And places, which this part found matter most for children. Each has its own costs and evidence, and each later part weighs them.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: distributional analysis.

Budget offices, treasuries and research institutes publish distributional tables for major tax and benefit changes: who gains and who loses, decile by decile. Here is one for the Island. A flat tax of 20 percent on every income, with the revenue paid back equally, 12,000 dollars a head. Rank people by pre-tax income and compute each decile's net gain. The poorest tenth gains 75 percent of its income; deciles 8 to ten pay, the top tenth 14 percent of its income. The Gini falls from 0.41 to 0.32. A flat tax with an equal grant is progressive: what matters is the whole system, not one rate.

Every such table rests on four choices, and readers should look for each. The unit: a person, a household or a tax unit, and how a family's needs are scaled to its size. The income: market income, pre-tax, or disposable, and whether capital gains and untaxed income count, the heart of chapter three's dispute. The ranking: by income before the policy or after it. And the measures: several, since they watch different parts of the distribution, each with its uncertainty.

And every number from a sample comes with uncertainty, largest at the top. With 2,000 of the Island's people, the Gini is 0.41, give or take two hundredths. With two hundred, the interval is twice as wide. The top one percent's share is harder: from two thousand people, twenty in the top percent, the interval spans several points; from two hundred, two people in the top percent, it is too wide to be useful. That is why top shares come from tax records, which cover everyone who files.
